authoredPrompt: This figure is a single pressure-temperature plot headed H2O. The vertical axis reads "Pressure, p (atm)" with ticks at 0.006, 1, and 218, and the horizontal axis reads "Temperature, T (C)" with ticks at 0, 0.01, 100, and 374, the spacing on both visibly nonlinear. Two red curves meet at a filled dot labeled "Triple point" at 0.006 atm and 0.01 degrees, with dashed guide lines running to both axes. From that dot one branch rises almost vertically and leans slightly left, while the other sweeps up and to the right, ending at a second filled dot labeled "Critical point" at 218 atm and 374 degrees; below the triple point a single curve continues toward the lower left. Italic letters mark the regions the curves carve out: s at the left, l in the wedge between the branches, and v at the right. Curved arrows tag the branches "Melting", "Boiling", and "Sublimation", and a dashed pair marks the crossing at 1 atm and 100 degrees. Locating a point against these curves tells the reader which phase water occupies there. The plot lays out the coexistence boundaries, including the leftward-leaning melting line whose negative slope means added pressure can melt ice.
authoredInteractions:
- Slider for temperature and pressure: the learner adjusts T and p controls, a state point moves across the diagram and the solid, liquid, or vapor region highlights, making clear that phase is determined by location relative to the coexistence curves.
- Slider for pressure near the melting boundary: the learner raises pressure along a fixed-temperature line close to 0 degrees C, the state point crosses the left-leaning melting curve and the phase label changes from solid to liquid, making clear why added pressure can melt ice.
- Toggle between heating paths: the learner switches among a 1 atm path, a low-pressure path through the triple point area, and a supercritical path, the crossed boundaries and transition labels appear, making clear how boiling, sublimation, and the critical point depend on the path through p-T space.
authoredContext:
The figure shows the phase diagram for water. Using the graph, if you know the pressure and temperature, you can determine the phase of water. The solid curves—boundaries between phases—indicate phase transitions, that is, temperatures and pressures at which the phases coexist. For example, the boiling point of water is 100°C at 1.00 atm. As the pressure increases, the boiling temperature rises gradually to 374°C at a pressure of 218 atm. A pressure cooker (or even a covered pot) cooks food faster than an open pot, because the water can exist as a liquid at temperatures greater than 100°C without all boiling away. (As we’ll see in the next section, liquid water conducts heat better than steam or hot air.) The boiling point curve ends at a certain point called the critical point—that is, a critical temperature, above which the liquid and gas phases cannot be distinguished; the substance is called a supercritical fluid. At sufficiently high pressure above the critical point, the gas has the density of a liquid but does not condense. Carbon dioxide, for example, is supercritical at all temperatures above 31.0°C. Critical pressure is the pressure of the critical point.

Similarly, the curve between the solid and liquid regions in the figure gives the melting temperature at various pressures. For example, the melting point is 0°C at 1.00 atm, as expected. Water has the unusual property that ice is less dense than liquid water at the melting point, so at a fixed temperature, you can change the phase from solid (ice) to liquid (water) by increasing the pressure. That is, the melting temperature of ice falls with increased pressure, as the phase diagram shows. For example, when a car is driven over snow, the increased pressure from the tires melts the snowflakes; afterwards, the water refreezes and forms an ice layer.

The phase diagram (pT graph) for water shows solid (s), liquid (l), and vapor (v) phases. At temperatures and pressure above those of the critical point, there is no distinction between liquid and vapor. Note that the axes are nonlinear and the graph is not to scale. This graph is simplified—it omits several exotic phases of ice at higher pressures. The phase diagram of water is unusual because the melting-point curve has a negative slope, showing that you can melt ice by increasing the pressure.

Graph of pressure P in atmosphere versus temperature T in degree Celsius for water. The curve starts with going up and right to a point labeled triple point. This is at 0.006 atm and 0.01 degree C. From here, the curve diverges into two branches. One goes up and left and is almost vertical. The other goes up and right. On the branch going up and right is a point at 1 atm and 100 degrees C. Further up on the same branch is a point labeled critical point. This is at 218 atm and 374 degrees C. The area to the left of the left branch is labeled solid. The area between two branches is labeled liquid. The area to the right of the right branch is labeled vapour. The curve to the lower left of the triple point is labeled sublimation, the branch to the upper left of the triple point is labeled melting, and the branch to the upper right of the triple point is labeled boiling.

discrepancies: The default figure adds a pale green liquid-region fill, a large green state point, and a bold 'liquid' label, none of which appear in the source static diagram and which change the clean black/red textbook look.
The generated diagram uses interactive colored phase highlighting for the active phase, whereas the source has unshaded white phase regions with only the italic s, l, and v labels.
The vaporization curve from 100 °C to the critical point is somewhat straighter and less smoothly bowed than the source curve.
The added current-state label competes visually with the original italic liquid-region label, making the central region more cluttered than in the source.
Some annotation placements differ: the critical-point label is shifted leftward relative to the source and the boiling arrow sits lower, though the targets remain understandable.
evaluation.notes: The main water phase-diagram geometry, key points, dashed guides, and labels are mostly faithful, but the default state-point overlay and colored phase fill make it less like the original clean textbook figure.
action_items: Hide the movable state point, its phase-name label, and the active-region fill by default, or make them appear only after the user changes a control.
Keep the default phase regions unfilled white so the red coexistence curves and black annotations match the source style.
Refine the liquid-vapor curve near the critical point to better match the source's smoother upward curvature.
Reduce clutter around the central liquid region by avoiding the extra 'liquid' label when the original italic 'l' is already present.
